summary: The new OCR, date‑picker and categories features do not introduce critical or high‑severity remote exploits, but several existing medium‑severity issues remain unaddressed and a couple of new medium‑severity concerns appear (CSV injection via custom category names and a potential ReDoS in receipt parsing). The data‑reset photo‑leak has been fixed. Dependency vulnerabilities remain and must be handled at deployment time.

findings.issue: CSV export does not fully escape user‑provided category names. A malicious custom category (e.g. starting with =, +, - or @) can trigger CSV injection when the CSV is opened in spreadsheet software.
findings.fix: Replace the ad‑hoc CSV builder with a library such as `csv-stringify` or implement RFC 4180‑compliant escaping for every field, including category values.

findings.issue: `parseReceipt` applies several regular expressions on the raw OCR text without input length limits. An attacker supplying a very large or specially crafted receipt string could cause catastrophic back‑tracking and freeze the UI (ReDoS).
findings.fix: Limit the maximum length of the OCR text processed (e.g., 10 KB) and use non‑catastrophic regex patterns; consider a line‑by‑line parse instead of large global matches.

findings.issue: Category names are only checked for a length of 1‑40 characters, but no sanitisation is performed. Certain Unicode control characters or line‑breaks could break CSV or PDF generation and UI layout.
findings.fix: Trim whitespace, reject control characters (e.g., \n, \r, \t) and normalise Unicode (NFC). Ensure the validated string is safe for all downstream formats.
